Adding a suitable unknot to any link
equates bridge number and meridional rank

Ryan Blair, Alexandra Kjuchukova and Ella Pfaff
Abstract.

Given any link L⊆S3L\subseteq S^{3}, we show that it is possible to embed an unknot UU in its complement so that the link L∪UL\cup U satisfies the Meridional Rank Conjecture (MRC). The bridge numbers in our construction fit into the equality β⁡(L∪U)=2​β​(L)−1=rank​(π1​(S3\(L∪U)))\beta(L\cup U)=2\beta(L)-1=\text{rank}(\pi_{1}(S^{3}\backslash(L\cup U))). In addition, we prove the MRC for new infinite families of links and distinguish them from previously settled cases through an application of bridge distance.

1. Introduction

Given a link L⊂S3L\subset S^{3}, we denote its bridge number and meridional rank by β⁡(L)\beta(L) and μ⁡(L)\mu(L), respectively. The meridional rank conjecture, or MRC, due to Cappell and Shaneson [Kir95, Problem 1.18], asks whether the equality β⁡(L)=μ⁡(L)\beta(L)=\mu(L) holds for every link in S3S^{3}. Over the last four decades, the conjecture has been established for many links satisfying a variety of geometric conditions [BZ85, RZ87, Bur88, BZ89, BDJW17, CH16, Cor14, BBK21, BK20, BBKM23, Dut22]. The analogous statement is also shown to hold for some knotted spheres in S4S^{4} [JP24]. One shared characteristic of the above diverse families is that all knots among them have low distance relative to their bridge number; specifically, for any knot covered by the results mentioned above, the ratio of bridge distance over bridge number is less than 3. In Proposition 1.4 and in Section 2.2, we give new families of links which satisfy MRC and which contain knots for which the bridge number and the ratio of bridge distance to bridge number can be arbitrarily high. The links we examine in this paper, which we call fishnets (see Definition 1.2 and Figure 1), can also be used to prove the following.

Theorem 1.1.

For any link L⊆S3L\subseteq S^{3} in bridge position with b>1b>1 bridges, there is an unknot U⊆S3\LU\subseteq S^{3}\backslash L such that

(1) β⁡(L∪U)=μ⁡(L∪U)=2​b−1=rank​(π1​(S3\(L∪U))).\beta(L\cup U)=\mu(L\cup U)=2b-1=\text{rank}(\pi_{1}(S^{3}\backslash(L\cup U))).

Given a link LL in bridge position with bb bridges, we describe an embedding of an unknot UU in the complement of LL so that Equation 1 holds. In our construction, a minimal generating set of meridians for L∪UL\cup U contains exactly bb meridians of LL. Moreover, it is in fact a minimal generating set for the group, without restricting the conjugacy classes of generators. Note that we allow bb to exceed β⁡(L)\beta(L), in which case the number of meridians of LL needed in a generating set for L∪UL\cup U exceeds β⁡(L)\beta(L).

The proof of Theorem 1.1 relies on finding maximal rank Coxeter quotients, in the sense studied in [BBK21, BBKM23, BKM24], of fundamental groups of fishnet link complements. A map from the group of a link LL onto a Coxeter group G⁡(Γ)G(\Gamma) is maximal rank if it maps meridians to reflections and the Coxeter rank of G⁡(Γ)G(\Gamma) is equal to (any upper bound on) the bridge number of LL. We define fishnet links as plat closures of braids which admit diagrams as in Figure 1. The bridge distance of what we call strong fishnet links was previously studied by Johnson and Moriah [JM16], and incompressible surfaces in the complement of fishnets was investigated by Finkelstein and Moriah [FM99a, FM99b]. By definition, a fishnet link LL is determined by a set of integer parameters corresponding to the powers of the standard braid generators in a fishnet diagram of LL. In Proposition 1.4, we give sufficient conditions, in terms of this parameter set, for a fishnet link LL to admit a maximal rank Coxeter quotient. In particular, we find infinite families of fishnets which satisfy MRC, with the properties discussed above.

Definition 1.2.

Given an integer valued vector

𝔱:=(t1,2,t1,4,…,t1,m−2,t2,1,t2,3,…,t2,m−1,…,tn,2,tn,4,…,tn,m−2),\mathfrak{t}:=(t_{1,2},t_{1,4},\dots,t_{1,m-2};t_{2,1},t_{2,3},\dots,t_{2,m-1};\dots;t_{n,2},t_{n,4},\dots,t_{n,m-2}),

let L𝔱L_{\mathfrak{t}} denote the plat closure of the mm-stranded braid

ζ𝔱:=(σ2t1,2​σ4t1,4​…​σm−2t1,m−2)​(σ1t2,1​σ3t2,3​…​σm−1t2,m−1)​(σ2t3,2​σ4t3,4​…​σm−2t3,m−2)​…​(σ2tn,2​σ4tn,4​…​σm−2tn,m−2).\zeta_{\mathfrak{t}}:=(\sigma_{2}^{t_{1,2}}\sigma_{4}^{t_{1,4}}\dots\sigma_{m-2}^{t_{1,m-2}})(\sigma_{1}^{t_{2,1}}\sigma_{3}^{t_{2,3}}\dots\sigma_{m-1}^{t_{2,m-1}})(\sigma_{2}^{t_{3,2}}\sigma_{4}^{t_{3,4}}\dots\sigma_{m-2}^{t_{3,m-2}})\dots(\sigma_{2}^{t_{n,2}}\sigma_{4}^{t_{n,4}}\dots\sigma_{m-2}^{t_{n,m-2}}).

(See Figure 1.) If all the integers ti,jt_{i,j} are non-zero, we say LL is a regular fishnet link, or simply a fishnet, of width mm and height nn. When |ti,j|≥3|t_{i,j}|\geq 3 for all i,j,i,j, we say LL is a strong fishnet. If some of the parameters ti,jt_{i,j} are 0, we say LL is a loose fishnet.

Remark 1.3.

By allowing sufficiently many ti,jt_{i,j} to be zero, we can present any link LL as a loose fishnet with width equal to 2​β​(L)2\beta(L). In other words, one can regard the symmetry imposed in fishnet diagrams as merely a convenient organizational principle applicable to all links.

We will refer to the collection of twist regions whose parameters are of the form ti,∗t_{i,\ast} as row ii of the fishnet; and to the the twist regions whose parameters are of the form t∗,jt_{\ast,j} as column jj. Note that the row indices in each column have the same parity; that the integer mm is always even while nn is always odd; and that a fishnet diagram is by definition in bridge position with m2\frac{m}{2} bridges. In what follows, it will be helpful to name the greatest common divisors of parameters which share a column, so we let d1,d2,…,dm−1d_{1},d_{2},\dots,d_{m{-}1} be the positive integers defined as follows:

(2) dj:=gcd1≤i≤nji≡j+1mod2⁡{ti,j},d_{j}:=\gcd_{\begin{subarray}{c}1\leq i\leq n_{j}\\ i\equiv j+1\mod 2\end{subarray}}\left\{t_{i,j}\right\},

where nj=n−1n_{j}=n-1 if jj is odd and nj=nn_{j}=n if jj is even. If for some j=kj=k we have that all parameters ti,kt_{i,k} in column kk are equal to zero, we use the convention that dk=∞d_{k}=\infty.

In the next theorem we use Coxeter quotients of link groups to derive sufficient conditions on the parameter vector 𝔱\mathfrak{t} which guarantee that the meridional rank of L𝔱L_{\mathfrak{t}} is also equal to m2\frac{m}{2}. As remarked above, these fishnets provide the first evidence that links which satisfy MRC are not limited to links which have bounded bridge number, bounded bridge distance, or bounded ratio of bridge distance over bridge number. See Theorem 4.5 for a discussion of these complexity measures for previously known cases.

Proposition 1.4.

Let L𝔱L_{\mathfrak{t}} denote the regular fishnet link determined by the parameter vector

𝔱:=(t1,2,t1,4,…,t1,m−2,t2,1,t2,3,…,t2,m−1,…,tn,2,tn,4,…,tn,m−2);\mathfrak{t}:=(t_{1,2},t_{1,4},\dots,t_{1,m-2};t_{2,1},t_{2,3},\dots,t_{2,m-1};\dots;t_{n,2},t_{n,4},\dots,t_{n,m-2});

and let d1,d2,…,dm−1d_{1},d_{2},\dots,d_{m{-}1} be as defined in Equation 2. If

d2​j>1​ for all ​1≤j≤m−22,d_{2j}>1\text{ for all }1\leq j\leq\frac{m-2}{2},

then μ⁡(L)=β⁡(L)=m2\mu(L)=\beta(L)=\frac{m}{2}. In particular, the MRC holds for LL. Moreover, if LL is a strong fishnet (that is, |ti,j|≥3,∀i,j|t_{i,j}|\geq 3,\forall i,j) and m≥6,m\geq 6, then LL has bridge distance ⌈n/(m−4))⌉\lceil n/(m-4))\rceil.

Corollary 1.5.

For any b∈ℕ≥3b\in\mathbb{N}_{\geq 3} and r∈ℝr\in\mathbb{R}, there exists a knot KK with β⁡(K)=μ⁡(K)=b\beta(K)=\mu(K)=b such that db>r,\frac{d}{b}>r, where dd is the bridge distance of K.K.

The proof of Theorem 1.4, given in Section 2.1, is a straightforward application of the technique introduced in [BBK21] and the main result in [JM16]. We also note that the above list of conditions is far from exhaustive. Other families of fishnets which satisfy MRC are given in Section 2.2. These generalize in obvious ways to produce additional examples with arbitrarily large bridge number and bridge distance. We have singled out the families in Proposition 1.4 only because these cases lend themselves to a particularly succinct description and proof; and because they are the ones needed in the proof of Theorem 1.1.

The rest of the paper is organized as follows. In Section 2, we prove Proposition 1.4 and we introduce other families of fishnets which admit maximal rank Coxeter quotients. Section 3 contains the proof of Theorem 1.1. In Section 4, we review the definition of bridge distance and prove Theorem 4.5, which states that knots for which MRC was previously established have either bounded bridge number, bounded distance, or bounded ratio of bridge distance over bridge number. Section 5 contains a brief conclusion.

2. Maximal Rank Coxeter Quotients of Fishnets

In this section, we prove Proposition 1.4 and Corollary 1.5; and we give some additional families of fishnet links which satisfy MRC. We also lay the groundwork for the proof of Theorem 1.1.

2.1. Maximal Rank Coxeter Quotients

Our technique throughout will be the following: given L𝔱L_{\mathfrak{t}} a loose fishnet of width mm, we will construct a quotient φ:π1​(S3∖L𝔱)→G𝔱,\varphi:\pi_{1}(S^{3}\setminus L_{\mathfrak{t}})\rightarrow G_{\mathfrak{t}}, where G𝔱G_{\mathfrak{t}} is a Coxeter group of Coxeter rank m2\frac{m}{2}. As the notation suggests, the group G𝔱G_{\mathfrak{t}} will be determined by the parameter vector 𝔱\mathfrak{t} which defines the fishnet. Note that φ\varphi will be a maximal rank Coxeter quotient in the sense of [BKM24]; in particular, φ\varphi maps meridians of L𝔱L_{\mathfrak{t}} to reflections of G𝔱G_{\mathfrak{t}}. Then, the Coxeter rank of G𝔱G_{\mathfrak{t}} is equal to the number of local maxima of L𝔱L_{\mathfrak{t}} depicted in Figure 1. Such a quotient gives a tight lower bound on the meridional rank of π1​(S3\L𝔱)\pi_{1}(S^{3}\backslash L_{\mathfrak{t}}), as in [BBK21, BBKM23], proving that β⁡(L)=μ⁡(L)=m2\beta(L)=\mu(L)=\frac{m}{2} as claimed.

We will represent quotients φ:π1​(S3\L𝔱)→G𝔱\varphi:\pi_{1}(S^{3}\backslash L_{\mathfrak{t}})\to G_{\mathfrak{t}} in a diagram DD of L𝔱L_{\mathfrak{t}} in the usual way, going back to Fox: by labeling strands in DD with the images of the corresponding Wirtinger meridians in G𝔱G_{\mathfrak{t}}. This labeling defines a quotient map iff at each crossing the image of the Wirtinger relation holds in G𝔱G_{\mathfrak{t}}. Given a twist region in DD, to determine the image of all strands in this region under φ,\varphi, it suffices to label the two strands incoming into the twist region from the top (resp. the bottom).

The following observations will be used repeatedly in the paper. Given any twist region σktj,k\sigma_{k}^{t_{j,k}} in the fishnet L𝔱L_{\mathfrak{t}}, let aa and bb denote the labels of the two incoming strands from the top and let rr denote the order of (a​b)(ab) in GG. If rr divides tj,k,t_{j,k}, then the Wirtinger meridians of the two outgoing strands are also labeled by aa and bb; moreover, aa and bb appear in the same order, left to right, at the top and the bottom of the twist region. If r=2r=2 (equivalently, aa and bb commute), then, regardless of whether rr divides tj,kt_{j,k}, the outgoing strands are again labeled aa and bb; the order in which the labels a,ba,b appear is determined by the parity of tj,kt_{j,k} in the obvious way. These diagrammatic constructions were inspired by Brunner [Bru92], who studied Artin quotients of link groups.

Proof of Proposition 1.4.

Consider the Coxeter group

G𝔱=⟨a1,a2,…,am2|a12=a22⋯=am22=1 and (ajaj+1)d2​j=1 for all j∈{1,…,m2−1}⟩.G_{\mathfrak{t}}=\left\langle a_{1},a_{2},\dots,a_{\frac{m}{2}}\ \big\lvert\ a_{1}^{2}=a_{2}^{2}\dots=a_{\frac{m}{2}}^{2}=1\text{ and }(a_{j}a_{j+1})^{d_{2j}}=1\text{ for all }j\in\{1,...,\tfrac{m}{2}{-}1\}\right\rangle.

Since dj>1d_{j}>1 for all j,j, it follows that G𝔱G_{\mathfrak{t}} has Coxeter rank equal to m2\frac{m}{2} [FT10, Lemma 2.1]. Let L𝔱L_{\mathfrak{t}} be represented in the fishnet diagram determined by the parameter vector 𝔱\mathfrak{t} in the sense of Definition 1.2. We begin by labeling the strands containing the m2\frac{m}{2} local maxima in the diagram by a1,a2,…,am2,a_{1},a_{2},\dots,a_{\frac{m}{2}}, in this order. Recall that, by assumption, for each jj, djd_{j} divides ti,j​∀it_{i,j}\ \forall i. Therefore, by the discussion above, for each twist region in the diagram, the labels of the incoming strands are the same as those of the outgoing strands. This implies that the induced labels at the two endpoints of a strand containing a local minimum agree. We have therefore arrived at a coherent coloring of the diagram by elements of the group G𝔱G_{\mathfrak{t}}. This defines the desired quotient φ:π1​(S3\L𝔱)→G𝔱\varphi:\pi_{1}(S^{3}\backslash L_{\mathfrak{t}})\to G_{\mathfrak{t}} of Coxeter rank m2\frac{m}{2}, proving the claim that β⁡(L𝔱)=μ⁡(L𝔱)=m2\beta(L_{\mathfrak{t}})=\mu(L_{\mathfrak{t}})=\frac{m}{2}.

To prove the final claim of the theorem, assume that the parameter vector 𝔱\mathfrak{t} satisfies |ti,j|≥3​∀i,j|t_{i,j}|\geq 3\ \forall i,j. Then, L𝔱L_{\mathfrak{t}} fulfills the hypotheses of Theorem 4.4. Therefore, the distance of the induced bridge sphere in the fishnet diagram is ⌈n/(m−4)⌉\lceil n/(m-4)\rceil. ∎

Proof of Corollary 1.5.

Fix r∈ℝ>0r\in\mathbb{R}_{>0} and b∈ℕ≥3b\in\mathbb{N}_{\geq 3}. Let L𝔱L_{\mathfrak{t}} be the fishnet determined by the parameter vector

𝔱=(t1,2,t1,4,…,t1,m−2,…,tn,m−2),\mathfrak{t}=(t_{1,2},t_{1,4},\dots,t_{1,m-2};\dots,t_{n,m{-}2}),

where m2=b≥3\frac{m}{2}=b\geq 3 and where we choose nn such that n≥r​m22.n\geq\frac{rm^{2}}{2}. In this construction, we may select the integer parameters freely, so we assume that ∀i,j\forall i,j, we have ti,j>3t_{i,j}>3 and d2​j>1d_{2j}>1. By Proposition 1.4, it follows that β⁡(L𝔱)=m2\beta(L_{\mathfrak{t}})=\frac{m}{2} and that d⁡(L𝔱)≥nm−4d(L_{\mathfrak{t}})\geq\frac{n}{m-4}. Thus, db≥nm−4⋅2m>r,\frac{d}{b}\geq\frac{n}{m-4}\cdot\frac{2}{m}>r, as claimed. To conclude the proof, note that by Lemma 3.1 we may furthermore ensure that L𝔱L_{\mathfrak{t}} is a knot. ∎

2.2. Other Fishnets which satisfy MRC

In what follows, we will work in the setting of loose fishnets. We will see in this section many new families of fishnets which admit maximal rank Coxeter quotients and thus satisfy MRC. We encourage the reader to understand these families as extensions of representative examples.

2.2.1. Decomposing Fishnets

The key observation is that the existence of a quotient for a fishnet L𝔱L_{\mathfrak{t}} can be detected by decomposing L𝔱L_{\mathfrak{t}} into a union of sublinks, L𝔱=⋃iLiL_{\mathfrak{t}}=\bigcup_{i}L_{i}. In particular, the LiL_{i} are not necessarily knots.

Consider the fishnet MM given by Figure 2. With the majority of boxes at most determined up to parity, MM does not necessarily satisfy the gcd condition of Proposition 1.4. However, MM admits a maximal rank Coxeter quotient. For fishnets of more than one component, it is common for the existence of a quotient to be dependent on relatively few parameters, as is the case for MM.

The colors in Figure 2 are included to guide the construction of the desired quotient. First, the faintly pictured sublink (colored so for diagrammatic clarity) is a 2-bridge link and therefore has a maximal rank Coxeter quotient given by a dihedral group. In this case, the quotient group is D11,D_{11}, the dihedral group of order 22. Next, consider the red/blue sublink. Because the red meets the blue in a single twist region, we regard each as a summand. If both summands admit maximal rank Coxeter quotients, then the red/blue sublink does as well. By assumption, the blue is a 2-bridge link summand, hence has some dihedral quotient, DbD_{b}. The red is a 3-bridge link summand, but due to the twist region parameterized by t4,2=1t_{4,2}=1, it fails the gcd condition given in Proposition 1.4 and does not have an obvious quotient. Instead, we consider the red summand along with the green unknot. Together these have 4-bridges, and in fact satisfy the gcd condition needed for the red/green to admit a maximal rank Coxeter quotient, Cr,gC_{r,g}. Moreover, the green does not meet the blue in any twist region, so we can regard the red/green and the blue as two summands of the red/green/blue link, summands which both admit maximal rank quotients. By reconciling these two quotient groups, we construct a maximal rank Coxeter quotient, Cr,g,bC_{r,g,b}, for the red/green/blue sublink. Acting by conjugation on Cr,gC_{r,g} and DbD_{b} ensures that two Coxeter generators, rr and bb, from Cr,gC_{r,g} and DbD_{b} respectively, label the strands entering the top of twist region t5,12=13t_{5,12}=13. Then, a minimal Coxeter generating set is given by the union of minimal Coxeter generating sets of Cr,gC_{r,g} and DbD_{b}; the relations are given by the union of relations for these two groups, together with the additional relation (r​b)13=1(rb)^{13}=1. At last, this results in the maximal rank Coxeter quotient for MM, CM=D11⊕Cr,g,bC_{M}=D_{11}\oplus C_{r,g,b}.

Note that none of the components of the link in the above example is presented in a diagram of a regular fishnet (not even the blue summand). Moreover, the example illustrates the following more general phenomena:

  1. (1)

    If kk disjoint sublinks of a link L=L1∪⋯∪LkL=L_{1}\cup\dots\cup L_{k} independently admit maximal rank11 1 In this context, “maximal” is meant in the following sense: the Coxeter rank of the quotient of LiL_{i} equals an upper bound on the bridge number of LiL_{i} as a sublink of LL, that is, the number of bridges that LiL_{i} contributes to LL. Coxeter quotients, G1,…,GkG_{1},\dots,G_{k}, then LL admits a maximal rank quotient onto the direct sum G:=G1⊕⋯⊕GkG:=G_{1}\oplus\dots\oplus G_{k}. The existence of a quotient π1​(S3\L)↠G\pi_{1}(S^{3}\backslash L)\twoheadrightarrow G is not affected by the way these sublinks link each other. In particular, they do not need to form a regular fishnet.

  2. (2)

    Our ability to detect the existence of a quotient in a fixed diagram may depend on the way we subdivide a link into a union of sublinks. For instance, if some component KsK_{s} of a link LL does not admit a maximal rank Coxeter quotient, it may still be the case that the link Ks∪KtK_{s}\cup K_{t} admits one, where KtK_{t} is some other component of LL which meets KsK_{s} in at least one twist region.

  3. (3)

    Let L1L_{1} and L2L_{2} form a split link, presented in a diagram such that L1L_{1} and L2L_{2} are contained in disjoint balls in the plane. Leaving all but two strands unchanged in the diagrams of L1L_{1} and L2L_{2}, we can obtain a diagram of a link of the form L1​#​T(2,t)​#​L2=:LL_{1}\#T_{(2,t)}\#L_{2}=:L, where T(2,t)T_{(2,t)} denotes the (2,t)(2,t)-torus link. If the initial diagrams D1,D2D_{1},D_{2} of L1,L2L_{1},L_{2} are (possibly loose) fishnets, it is easy to obtain a (necessarily loose) fishnet diagram for LL: simply juxtapose D1D_{1} and D2D_{2} and insert a new column between them, in which one parameter is equal to tt and the remaining are equal to zero. (When L1L_{1} and L2L_{2} have different height, rows of zeroes are added to either D1D_{1} or D2D_{2}.) In particular, if L1L_{1} and L2L_{2} admit quotients onto the Coxeter groups G1G_{1} and G2G_{2}, then LL admits a quotient onto a Coxeter group determined by G1G_{1}, G2G_{2}, and tt in the natural way.

Using the above remarks, one readily constructs new families of links which admit maximal rank Coxeter quotients. In particular, one can build regular fishnets of arbitrary dimensions which admit “nonobvious” Coxeter quotients and satisfy MRC.

2.2.2. Combining Fishnets

In Figure 3 we introduce the key construction used in Section 3.

We start with two fishnets, L1L_{1} and L2L_{2}, in bridge position with bb and b−1b-1 bridges, respectively; they may have any number of rows22 2 This may not be immediately apparent from Figure 3. If one of the sublinks, LiL_{i}, has fewer rows than the other, we add rows of boxes labeled “0” to LiL_{i} until the heights of the two links match. Then L1L_{1} and L2L_{2} can be interweaved. A similar idea is presented in Figure 4, in which the process described for LiL_{i} is applied to the blue sublink.. The two links are depicted, superimposed, in Figure 3. L1L_{1} is black, L2L_{2} is blue. When the diagrams are simply placed on top of each other, the gray boxes contain single crossings. We use this setup to construct new families of fishnets in (2​b−1)(2b-1)-bridge position by changing the values of the parameters in the gray boxes. We study the existence of Coxeter quotients of Coxeter rank 2​b−12b-1 for these fishnets.

As in observation (1) above, if sublinks L1L_{1} and L2L_{2} admit Coxeter quotients of rank bb and b−1b-1, then LL admits a maximal rank Coxeter quotient given by the direct sum of these two. Unique to this arrangement is that LL may be constructed so that it admits a maximal rank quotient regardless of whether sublinks L1L_{1} and L2L_{2} do. Indeed, the gcd condition of Proposition 1.4 — namely dj>1d_{j}>1 for all even jj — depends only on parameters of LL which are in gray boxes in Figure 3. These parameters are fixed mod 2 in order to maintain the sublink decomposition of LL into L1L_{1} and L2L_{2}, but can always be chosen to satisfy this gcd condition in a way that preserves parity. Therefore, there is always a choice in the construction of LL which ensures L1∪L2L_{1}\cup L_{2} admits a maximal rank Coxeter quotient.

3. Proof of Theorem 1.1

This section presents the proof of Theorem 1.1. In Section 3.1 we give some preliminaries; and in Section 3.2 we give the full construction.

3.1. Component Number of Fishnets

We begin with a discussion of the component number of a fishnet. This will be used to demonstrate that the links which satisfy the hypotheses of Proposition 1.4 can have any number of components between 1 and the bridge number.

Let L𝔱L_{\mathfrak{t}} denote a loose fishnet which is the plat closure of an mm-stranded braid ζ𝔱\zeta_{\mathfrak{t}}. Consider the homomorphism ϕ:Bm↠Sm\phi:B_{m}\twoheadrightarrow S_{m} from the braid group to the symmetric group given by ϕ:σi↦(i​i+1)\phi:\sigma_{i}\mapsto(i~i{+}1). Using this map, we associate a permutation ϕ⁡(ζ𝔱)\phi(\zeta_{\mathfrak{t}}) to L𝔱L_{\mathfrak{t}} which can be used to obtain the component number of L𝔱L_{\mathfrak{t}}.

We will show that any component number between 1 and m2\frac{m}{2} can be achieved by a fishnet of width mm satisfying a prescribed gcd condition on the parameters in even columns. Precisely, fix any even integer m≥2m\geq 2 and any set of odd integers δ2,δ4​…,δm\delta_{2},\delta_{4}\dots,\delta_{m}. The following lemma shows that there exists a transitive permutation in SmS_{m} which is in the image of a fishnet L𝔱L_{\mathfrak{t}}, whose parameter set 𝔱\mathfrak{t} has the property that d2​jd_{2j} is divisible by δ2​j\delta_{2j} for all j=1,2,…,m2j=1,2,\dots,\frac{m}{2}.

Lemma 3.1.

[Pfa24] Fix m∈ℕm\in\mathbb{N}, and fix set Δ={δ2,δ4,…,δm−2}\Delta=\{\delta_{2},\delta_{4},\dots,\delta_{m{-}2}\} such that δ2​j≥3\delta_{2j}\geq 3 and δ2​j≡1mod2\delta_{2j}\equiv 1\mod~2 for all δ2​j∈Δ\delta_{2j}\in\Delta. Let ℒΔ\mathcal{L}_{\Delta} be the set of strong fishnets L𝔱L_{\mathfrak{t}} defined by

3.2. Proof of Theorem 1.1

Let LL be a link in bridge position with bb bridges, presented in a diagram DD with bb local maxima with respect to the yy-axis in the plane of projection. Note that we do not require b=β⁡(L)b=\beta(L) and indeed our argument applies to any link in any bridge position, except the case where LL is an unknot and b=β⁡(L)=1b=\beta(L)=1.

Our proof can be split into two steps. First, we use DD to construct a new diagram, D′D^{\prime}, of LL such that D′D^{\prime} is a loose fishnet of width 2​b2b. We note that in most cases the process of obtaining D′D^{\prime} increases the crossing number. The second step is to interweave U,U, an unknot in bridge position with b−1b-1 bridges, through D′D^{\prime} to obtain the desired link L∪U.L\cup U.

Step one. A sequence of planar isotopies and Reidemeister II moves (potentially increasing the crossing number) transforms DD into a diagram D1D_{1} which is the plat closure of a braid. Moreover, we can assume that all local maxima of D1D_{1} are at the same height, say y=ay=a, and similarly, that all local minima are at the same height, y=by=b. We require that all crossings be at different heights between aa and bb, so that we can read off a braid word ζ∗=σi1r1​σi2r2​…​σikrk\zeta^{\ast}=\sigma_{i_{1}}^{r_{1}}\sigma_{i_{2}}^{r_{2}}\dots\sigma_{i_{k}}^{r_{k}} from D1D_{1}. We assume that ζ∗\zeta^{\ast} is reduced in the sense that ij≠ij+1i_{j}\neq i_{j+1} for all j.j.

In our construction, for each j=1,2,…,k−1,j=1,2,\dots,k{-}1, the term σijrj\sigma_{i_{j}}^{r_{j}} in ζ∗\zeta^{\ast} will take up two rows in a loose fishnet diagram of LL. The last term, σikrk\sigma_{i_{k}}^{r_{k}}, will take up a single row. As a result, there will be 2​k−12k-1 rows in the diagram constructed, of which k−1k-1 rows will consist entirely of zeroes. Clearly, when k>1k>1 the fishnet produced in this manner will not have minimal height. This inefficiency does not increase the bridge number of L∪UL\cup U, so we do not strive for minimality.

Consider σi1r1\sigma_{i_{1}}^{r_{1}}. It will contribute a box labeled r1r_{1} in column i1i_{1}. This box will be either in row 11 or in row 2,2, depending on the parity of i1i_{1}. The remaining parameters in the first two rows will be zero. We proceed in the same manner for all j<kj<k. That is, σijrj\sigma_{i_{j}}^{r_{j}} determines rows 2​j−12j-1 and 2​j2j. Again, all entries in these rows are zero, except for the entry in column ij,i_{j}, which is equal to rjr_{j}.

Without loss of generality, we may assume that iki_{k} is even. (If it is odd, then the plat closures of σi1r1​σi2r2​…​σikrk\sigma_{i_{1}}^{r_{1}}\sigma_{i_{2}}^{r_{2}}\dots\sigma_{i_{k}}^{r_{k}} and σi1r1​σi2r2​…​σik−1rk−1\sigma_{i_{1}}^{r_{1}}\sigma_{i_{2}}^{r_{2}}\dots\sigma_{i_{k-1}}^{r_{k{-}1}} represent the same link.) The last, (2​k−1)(2k-1)-th, row of D′D^{\prime} will then consist of rkr_{k} in the iki_{k}-th column and zeroes in the other columns. We do not follow this by a row of zeroes. This completes the construction of a loose fishnet diagram D′D^{\prime} for L.L.

Step two. Having presented LL as a loose fishnet, we now let the diagram D′D^{\prime} play the role of the black sublink in Figure 4. Remark 3.3.

Given a link L⊂S3L\subset S^{3}, let E⁡(L)E(L) denote its exterior. Putting these together, we have β⁡(L)≥g⁡(E⁡(L))=t⁡(L)+1≥rank⁡(π1​(S3\L)).\beta(L)\geq g(E(L))=t(L)+1\geq{\rm rank}(\pi_{1}(S^{3}\backslash L)). 4. Distance

Suppose MM is a compact, orientable 3-manifold containing a properly embedded, compact, 1-manifold τ\tau. In what follows, we consider properly embedded, compact surfaces F⊂MF\subset M which are transverse to τ\tau. The points τ∩F\tau\cap F are the punctures on FF. Two properly embedded punctured surfaces in MM are equivalent if they are properly isotopic via an isotopy that at every stage produces a surface transverse to τ\tau. We say two equivalent surfaces are transversely isotopic with respect to τ\tau (or simply that they are isotopic, if both transversality and τ\tau are understood from context). A curve γ⊂F\gamma\subset F will be called essential if γ\gamma is disjoint from τ\tau, is not boundary parallel, and doesn’t bound a disk in FF with fewer than two punctures. The surface FF is incompressible in MM if there is no disk DD (called a compressing disk) in M\τM\backslash\tau such that D∩F=∂DD\cap F=\partial D is an essential curve in FF. If FF is a sphere, it is called an inessential sphere if it bounds a ball disjoint from τ\tau or bounds a ball containing a single, boundary parallel subarc of τ\tau. A connected incompressible surface FF will be called essential if it is not an inessential sphere and if there is no parallelism transverse to τ\tau between FF and some collection of components of ∂M\partial M. If FF is a closed, connected, punctured separating surface in MM, then FF is bicompressible if there exists a compressing disk for FF contained to each of its sides.

A tangle (B,τ)(B,\tau) consists of a 3-ball BB and a properly embedded finite collection of arcs, τ\tau. A tangle (B,τ)(B,\tau) is irreducible if every unpunctured 2-sphere in (B,τ)(B,\tau) is inessential. The tangle (B,τ)(B,\tau) is trivial if there is a collection of disjoint compressing disks for ∂B\partial B contained in the complement of τ\tau so that surgering BB along this collection results in components that are 3-balls, each containing a single boundary parallel arc.

Recall that an nn-bridge sphere, Σ\Sigma, for a link LL in S3S^{3} is a sphere meeting LL transversely in 2​n2n points and dividing (S3,L)(S^{3},L) into two trivial tangles. The bridge spheres considered are not necessarily minimal. Note that when β⁡(L)=n,\beta(L)=n, there is an nn-bridge sphere Σ\Sigma for a representative of LL, and we say that Σ\Sigma realizes the bridge number of LL.

4.1. Distance

Distance is a complexity measure for bridge spheres, obtained from the distance between disk sets in the curve complex. Let L⊂S3L\subset S^{3} be a link and let Σ\Sigma be any bridge sphere for LL separating S3S^{3} into balls B1B_{1} and B2B_{2}. Define the curve complex of Σ\Sigma, denoted 𝒞⁡(Σ)\mathcal{C}(\Sigma), to be the graph whose vertices are isotopy classes of essential simple closed curves in Σ\Sigma. Two vertices are connected by an edge if their corresponding curves can be isotoped in Σ\L\Sigma\backslash L to be disjoint. We endow the vertex set of the curve complex 𝒞⁡(Σ)\mathcal{C}(\Sigma) with a metric in the natural way: assign length one to each edge and let the distance between two vertices be the length of the shortest path between them. Let the disk set, 𝒟i⊂𝒞⁡(Σ)\mathcal{D}_{i}\subset\mathcal{C}(\Sigma), be the set of vertices in 𝒞⁡(Σ)\mathcal{C}(\Sigma) which correspond to essential curves in Σ\Sigma that bound compressing disks in BiB_{i}, i=1,2i=1,2. We define the distance of Σ\Sigma, denoted d⁡(Σ)d(\Sigma), to be

d⁡(Σ)=min⁡{d⁡(c1,c2):ci∈𝒟i}.d(\Sigma)=\min\{d(c_{1},c_{2}):c_{i}\in\mathcal{D}_{i}\}.

If Σ\Sigma is punctured four or fewer times (i.e., when the curve complex is empty or disconnected), we define the distance of Σ\Sigma to be infinite. The distance of LL, d⁡(L)d(L), is the maximum possible distance d⁡(Σ)d(\Sigma) of any bridge sphere Σ\Sigma for a representative of LL such that Σ\Sigma realizes the bridge number of LL. It follows from [Tom07] that as long as β⁡(L)≥3\beta(L)\geq 3, this maximum is a well-defined positive integer.

Given a bridge sphere Σ\Sigma for a link LL, several authors have given upper bounds on the distance of Σ\Sigma in terms of the topology of certain essential [BS05, BCJ+17] or bi-compressible [Tom07, BCJ+17] surfaces in the link exterior. For simplicity, we have restricted ourselves to considering only knots and using only three such results when proving Theorem 4.5. We remark that some of the bounds on distance in Theorem 4.5 can be improved by employing lengthier arguments or alternative upper bounds on distance.

First, we need an upper bound on the distance of a knot in terms of the genus and number of boundary components of an essential (possibly meridional) surface in the knot exterior. The following theorem is a restatement of Theorem 5.7 of  [Tom07] for knots in S3S^{3}. This is very similar to the main theorem of [BS05], which uses a slightly different definition of distance. In the following theorem, E⁡(L)E(L) denotes the exterior of a link LL in S3S^{3}.

Theorem 4.1.

[Tom07, BS05] Suppose that LL is a non-trivial knot in S3S^{3}. Let Σ\Sigma be a bridge sphere for LL. Suppose that S¯⊂S3\overline{S}\subset S^{3} is a surface transverse to LL such that S=S¯∩E⁡(L)S=\overline{S}\cap E(L) is not a sphere and is essential in E⁡(L)E(L). Then

d⁡(Σ)≤max⁡{3,2​g​(S)+|S¯∩L|}.d(\Sigma)\leq\max\{3,2g(S)+|\overline{S}\cap L|\}.

If, in addition, S¯=S\overline{S}=S and if SS is a torus, then d⁡(Σ)≤2d(\Sigma)\leq 2.

Next, we need an upper bound on the distance of a knot in terms of the genus and number of boundary components of an essential surface with non-meridional boundary components. The following theorem is a specialization of Theorem 5.2 of [BCJ+17] to knots in S3S^{3}.

Theorem 4.2.

[BCJ+17] Let KK be a nontrivial knot in S3S^{3} with β⁡(K)≥3\beta(K)\geq 3. Suppose that FF is an orientable essential surface properly embedded in the exterior of KK with non-empty, non-meridional boundary. Then

β⁡(K)​(d⁡(K)−4)≤8​g​(F)−8|∂F|+4.\beta(K)(d(K)-4)\leq\frac{8g(F)-8}{|\partial F|}+4.

Finally, we need an upper bound on the distance of a knot in terms of the Heegaard genus of a manifold obtained by Dehn surgery. The following theorem is a specialization of Theorem 8.2 in [BCJ+17] to knots in S3S^{3}.

Theorem 4.3.

[BCJ+17] Let KK be a non-trivial knot in S3S^{3}. Let M′M^{\prime} be the result of non-trivial Dehn surgery on KK and let gg be the Heegaard genus of M′M^{\prime}. Then

d⁡(K)≤max⁡{2β⁡(K)+4,4​gβ⁡(K)+4,2​g+2}.d(K)\leq\max\Big\{\frac{2}{\beta(K)}+4,\frac{4g}{\beta(K)}+4,2g+2\Big\}.

4.2. Distance and Fishnet Links

In [JM16], Johnson and Moriah study the distance of strong fishnet links, described in the language of 2​k2k-plat projections. Given a diagram of a fishnet link as depicted in Figure 1, a horizontal line in the plane of projection that separates all maxima from all minima naturally corresponds to a bridge plane for the knot in ℝ3\mathbb{R}^{3}, or, equivalently, a bridge sphere for the knot in S3S^{3}. We call any bridge sphere transversely isotopic to this the induced bridge sphere for a fishnet link. Denote by ⌈x⌉\lceil x\rceil the ceiling function on xx, equal to the smallest integer greater than or equal to xx. Johnson and Moriah showed the following:

Theorem 4.4.

[JM16] If K⊂S3K\subset S^{3} is a strong fishnet link of width mm and height nn, then d⁡(Σ)=⌈n/(m−4)⌉d(\Sigma)=\lceil n/(m-4)\rceil, where Σ\Sigma is the induced bridge sphere.

4.3. Distance and classes of links known to satisfy the MRC

In this section we show that knots for which the MRC has previously been established have either small bridge number or the property that the ratio of their bridge distance over their bridge number is less than 3. We have restricted ourselves to knots here. That said, the tools used would apply to links in all cases except generalized Montesinos links [LM93], for which our proof would require a version of Theorem 4.3 for links. That said, we believe that Theorem 4.5 holds for links as well.

Theorem 4.5.

Let KK be a knot shown to satisfy the MRC in one of  [BZ85, RZ87, BZ89, LM93, CH16, Cor14, BDJW17, BK20, BBK21, BBKM23, Dut22]. Then either β⁡(K)≤5\beta(K)\leq 5 or d⁡(K)≤m​a​x​(8,2​β​(K)+2)d(K)\leq max(8,2\beta(K)+2).

Proof.

In  [BZ85],  [BBK21], and  [BBKM23], the authors prove the MRC for classes of Montesinos and arborescent knots. Every knot in these classes has the property that it is either bridge number at most 3 or that its exterior contains an essential meridional 4-punctured sphere. In the latter case, the distance of the knot is less than or equal to 4 by Theorem 4.1.

In  [RZ87],  [BZ89],  [Cor14],  [CH16],  [BDJW17],  [BK20], and  [Dut22], the authors prove the MRC for classes of 33-bridge knots, torus knots or satellite knots. Every knot in these classes has one or more of the following properties: its bridge number is at most 3, its exterior contains an essential non-meridional annulus, or its exterior contains an essential torus. In each of the latter two cases, the distance of the knot is less than or equal to three by Theorems 4.2 and 4.1.

In  [LM93], the authors prove the MRC for a class of knots known as “generalized Motesinos knots”. As a consequence of Theorem 0.1 in that same paper, every generalized Motesinos knot KK which the authors show satisfies the MRC additionally admits a non-trivial Dehn surgery resulting in a 3-manifold M⁡(K)M(K) such that the Heegaard genus of M⁡(K)M(K) is equal to β⁡(K)\beta(K). However, by Theorem 4.3, this non-trivial Dehn surgery implies that the distance of KK is at most the maximum of 88 and 2​β​(K)+22\beta(K)+2.

A second class of knots which the authors of  [BBK21] prove satisfy the MRC are twisted links. Here we will give a brief overview of the construction of these links (restricting our attention to knots). For additional details, we refer the reader to  [Bru92], where twisted links were introduced; and to [BBK21], where they were shown to satisfy MRC.

Let DD be a diagram of a knot LL, and let FF be one of the two surfaces with boundary LL obtained from a checkerboard coloring of the regions in the plane determined by DD. We regard the surface FF as a union of disks and twisted bands. We assume DD is reduced in the sense that it does not contain any nugatory crossings and that the sign of crossings in each band of FF is constant. When every band of FF is maximal (i.e. no disk is incident to exactly two bands) and contains at least one full twist, we call FF a twisted surface. A diagram DD is twisted if it determines such a surface via a checkerboard coloring, and a knot is twisted if it admits a twisted diagram. For instance, the standard diagram of the P⁡(a1,a2,…,an)P(a_{1},a_{2},\dots,a_{n}) pretzel knot is twisted so long as each aia_{i} satisfies |ai|>1|a_{i}|>1.

Retract the spanning surface FF to a planar graph Γ\Gamma, where vertices of Γ\Gamma represent disks of FF and edges represent bands of FF. The edges of Γ\Gamma are weighted with the number of half-twists in the corresponding band of FF. Denote the dual weighted planar graph by Γ∗\Gamma^{\ast}, where each edge of Γ∗\Gamma^{\ast} inherits the weight of the corresponding edge of Γ\Gamma. The surface FF is twisted if and only if all weights of Γ\Gamma are at least 2 in absolute value and Γ\Gamma has no vertices of valence one or two; LL is then a twisted knot. In  [BBK21], the authors prove the MRC for twisted knots, and they show that the bridge number of a twisted knot LL is equal to the number of vertices in Γ∗\Gamma^{\ast}.

Let KK be a twisted knot, let v∗v^{*} be the number of vertices in Γ∗\Gamma^{\ast}, and let v,e,fv,e,f be the number of vertices, edges, and faces, respectively, of the planar embedding of Γ\Gamma induced by FF. Then f=v∗f=v^{*} and 2=v−e+v∗2=v-e+v^{*}. Since FF retracts to Γ\Gamma, then χ⁡(F)=v−e\chi(F)=v-e and 2=χ⁡(F)+v∗2=\chi(F)+v^{*}. Since v∗=β⁡(K)v^{*}=\beta(K) by [BBK21], we have that

(4) χ⁡(F)=2−β⁡(K).\chi(F)=2-\beta(K).

If FF is orientable, then maximally compressing FF results in an essential Seifert surface, FcF^{c}, with genus at most the genus of FF and with one, non-meridional, boundary component. By Theorem 4.2, β⁡(K)≤5\beta(K)\leq 5, or d⁡(K)≤8​g​(Fc)−85​|∂Fc|+45+4≤2​g​(F)+165d(K)\leq\frac{8g(F^{c})-8}{5|\partial F^{c}|}+\frac{4}{5}+4\leq 2g(F)+\frac{16}{5}. Since d⁡(K)d(K) is an integer, d⁡(K)≤2​g​(F)+3d(K)\leq 2g(F)+3. Since g​(F)=12​(1−χ​(F))g(F)=\frac{1}{2}(1-\chi(F)), using Equation 4 we conclude that d⁡(K)≤β⁡(K)+2d(K)\leq\beta(K)+2.

If FF is non-orientable, we can use a similar construction. Let HFH_{F} be a closed regular neighborhood of FF in S3S^{3}. So, HFH_{F} is a handlebody of genus 1−χ⁡(Γ)=1−χ⁡(F)1-\chi(\Gamma)=1-\chi(F). Since KK can be assumed to lie in the surface ∂HF\partial H_{F}, we have that ∂HF\partial H_{F} meets a neighborhood of KK in exactly one annulus, denoted AA. Hence F′:=∂HF∖i​n​t​(A)F^{\prime}:=\partial H_{F}\setminus int(A) is a compact, connected, orientable surface properly embedded in the exterior of KK. Since F′F^{\prime} is obtained from ∂HF\partial H_{F} by deleting an annulus whose core is non-separating in ∂HF\partial H_{F}, we obtain g⁡(F′)=g⁡(∂HF)−1=−χ⁡(F)g(F^{\prime})=g(\partial H_{F})-1=-\chi(F). Moreover, F′F^{\prime} has two boundary components. Note that F′F^{\prime} may be compressible. Maximally compressing F′F^{\prime} in the exterior of LL produces an essential surface F′′F^{\prime\prime} with genus at most −χ⁡(F)-\chi(F) and with at most two boundary components. If β⁡(K)≤5\beta(K)\leq 5, then the theorem follows. So, we will assume β⁡(K)≥6\beta(K)\geq 6. By Theorem 4.2, β⁡(K)​(d⁡(K)−4)≤8​g​(F′′)−8|∂F′′|+4.\beta(K)(d(K)-4)\leq\frac{8g(F^{\prime\prime})-8}{|\partial F^{\prime\prime}|}+4. Since β⁡(K)≥6\beta(K)\geq 6, d⁡(K)≤8​g​(F′′)−86​|∂F′′|+143d(K)\leq\frac{8g(F^{\prime\prime})-8}{6|\partial F^{\prime\prime}|}+\frac{14}{3}. Since 1≤|∂F′′|≤21\leq|\partial F^{\prime\prime}|\leq 2, then d⁡(K)≤8​g​(F′′)−86+143=43​g​(F′′)+103.d(K)\leq\frac{8g(F^{\prime\prime})-8}{6}+\frac{14}{3}=\frac{4}{3}g(F^{\prime\prime})+\frac{10}{3}. Since g⁡(F′′)≤−χ⁡(F)=β⁡(K)−2g(F^{\prime\prime})\leq-\chi(F)=\beta(K)-2, then d⁡(K)≤43​β​(K)+23d(K)\leq\frac{4}{3}\beta(K)+\frac{2}{3}. ∎

5. Swimming with the Fishnets

Any link hanging down from a bridge
Can be a fishnet: jump in and — sea! —
Spin an icy unknot
Shivers get got
Swim in the unknot to catch MRC
